questions.q: What single pattern does this lesson say recurred across all eight Chapter 1 case studies, underneath their different Salesforce objects?
options: Every case required building a custom object
Every case was ultimately solved the same way, using identical configuration
Every case required moving to a new Salesforce license tier
Separating what shape a thing takes from who gets to see or touch it, and not letting a vague request stand in for the specific requirement underneath it
questions.explain: Record type vs. sharing rule, license tier vs. sharing set, work rule vs. service objective — each case repeated the same underlying habit: separate shape from visibility, and extract the real requirement from the vague ask, rather than reusing identical configuration across cases.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does it mean if you can't point to all five Chapter 2 skills (extraction, alternatives, risks, presentation, feedback) inside a Chapter 1 case without rereading it?
options: It means the case was absorbed as a solution to memorize rather than as reasoning that was internalized
It means the case was poorly written and should be skipped
It means that particular case didn't actually use any of the five skills
It means the student should retake the course from Lesson 1
questions.explain: Each Chapter 1 case was secretly practicing all five skills before they were named explicitly. Being unable to identify them without rereading suggests the case was memorized as a specific solution rather than internalized as a transferable reasoning pattern.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the course deliberately went one lesson deep on eight domains rather than many lessons deep on one?
options: Because Salesforce only allows eight architecture domains to exist
Because the transferable habit of mind across domains is the point of this course, not mastery of any single domain's full mechanics
Because deeper domain courses don't exist anywhere in this catalog
Because one-lesson-per-domain is a technical limitation of the course platform
questions.explain: This course is explicitly a survey built to practice a transferable reasoning habit across many domains; the catalog's other dedicated courses (sharing and visibility, integration architecture, enterprise data architecture, and this course's own Integration Architecture Case Studies sibling) go deeper on each specific domain's full mechanics.

questions.q: What makes Lesson 16's Lab different from every other Lab in this course?
options: It requires no written answer at all
It is the only Lab that has a single correct numeric answer
It asks the student to apply the full method to a real request from their own life, rather than to one of the course's fictional companies
It requires access to a live Salesforce org
questions.explain: Every other Lab in the course works through a fictional company's scenario. This final Lab deliberately asks the student to apply the extraction-alternatives-risks-presentation method to something real they've personally encountered, as the actual test of whether the method transfers.

questions.q: What does this lesson say separates an architect who solves the problem a stakeholder stated from one who solves the problem the stakeholder actually has?
options: Years of Salesforce certification alone
Avoiding all contact with business stakeholders and working directly from written tickets only
Always agreeing with whatever the first stakeholder request says

Consistently asking what the person is actually experiencing, what would count as fixed, what's being assumed, and whether a solution is hiding inside the ask — before treating the stated ask as the requirement
questions.explain: The lesson restates Lesson 9's extraction questions as the habit that separates the two kinds of architect — consistently interrogating a vague ask before treating its literal wording as the real requirement, which every case in the course demonstrated was necessary at least once.
